findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix D Performance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Leisure centre attendance in sustained decline, third consecutive quarterly drop at The Bridge
findings.detail: Attendance at council-owned leisure centres is 274,234 for Q1, below the target range (275,996–288,896). The Bridge (Horsham's main centre) has now experienced three consecutive quarters of decline versus the prior year, attributed to competition from the nearby commercial PureGym facility in Broadbridge Heath. Only a recording process improvement at Pavilion in the Park offset losses elsewhere. This reflects revenue pressure on council leisure services.
findings.matters: Leisure services often rely on commercial revenue to offset costs; sustained decline either reduces income or increases subsidy requirement. The Council is mid-procurement (20% complete) for a new leisure management contract, which may restructure these services.
findings.figures: 274,234 attendance (target range 275,996–288,896); 1% lower than Q1 2025/26; three consecutive quarters of decline at The Bridge

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix D Performance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate falls below prior year as cost-of-living pressures bite residents
findings.detail: In-year council tax collection rate is 28.85%, below both the target of 28.97% and the 29.15% achieved in the same quarter last year. The council attributes this to external economic pressures reducing residents' ability to pay, and notes increased requests for payment arrangements and support schemes. Recovery processes are being closely monitored but the trajectory is downward.
findings.matters: Council tax is the largest source of council revenue; collection below target reduces near-term cash and may require use of reserves or adjustment of spending forecasts.
findings.figures: 28.85% in-year collection (target 28.97%; prior year 29.15%)
findings.quote: The collection rate is currently below the level achieved at the same point last year. This reflects external economic pressures that have impacted customers' ability to pay and the speed at which debt can be recovered.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix D Performance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: B&B accommodation numbers surge above target as Section 21 notices precede eviction ban
findings.detail: Households in B&B accommodation reached 37 in Q1, 23% above the target of 30. The council explicitly attributes this to a spike in Section 21 notices issued before they were outlawed on 1 May 2026. The team notes housing services are seeing more complex cases involving domestic abuse, asylum seekers, care leavers and rough sleepers. While they state cases are manageable, the trajectory and complexity of need will drive accommodation spending.
findings.matters: B&B accommodation is expensive and non-permanent; this is demand-driven spending that increases council liabilities. The underlying cause (eviction notices) is time-limited but signals prior distress in the local housing market.
findings.figures: 37 households in B&B (target 30); 153 households in temporary accommodation (target 150); seven households due to move from B&B in Q2
findings.quote: We are experiencing an increase in workload as a result of an increase in the number of Section 21 notices issued before they were outlawed on 1 May 2026 through the Renters Rights Act. Despite the increase in cases, the team are able to manage the additional cases, limiting the use B&B wherever possible whilst fulfilling our statutory obligations.

findings.paper_title: Appendic A Annual Governance Statement 2025-26._Redacted
findings.headline: Multiple data handling incidents within 2025/26 reveal operational control gaps in data security
findings.detail: The council had two significant data handling breaches. A Planning mail merge sent an email with over 200 recipients without blind copy. Further training was provided, but the incidents indicate control gaps in data handling procedures.
findings.matters: Data handling failures create GDPR compliance risk and demonstrate control gaps in operational procedures that could result in financial or reputational loss and regulatory action.
findings.figures: Over 200 email addresses sent without blind copy in second incident
findings.quote: File sent to an incorrect email address containing some bank details and names. The email was deleted by the customer who had brought it to our attention. It was reported to the ICO who came back with some reminders of best practice to check before sending. An incorrect Planning mail merge process sent an email with over 200 email addresses that were not blind copied. Further training has been provided.

findings.paper_title: Appendic A Annual Governance Statement 2025-26._Redacted
findings.headline: Capitol Theatre roof procurement bypassed governance procedures and lacked adequate contract oversight
findings.detail: The council undertook procurement 'at pace' for the theatre's reopening deadline, leading to governance bypasses. Risk management was inadequate, procurement team consultation limited, only 'tacit approval' obtained for the exemption, the final contract was delayed, and a subsequent contract modification lacked sufficient senior management oversight per the Council's Procurement Code.
findings.matters: Demonstrates governance and control weaknesses in how the council manages capital projects and procurement, affecting ability to deliver capital schemes efficiently and with proper oversight.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: A procurement process was undertaken by Property on the Capitol Theatre roof at pace to meet the crucial reopening dates for the theatre. Some of the risks during that process were not managed as robustly as they could have been. The contract value was below the threshold at which a full procurement exercise is required under the Procurement Act, but consultation with the local Procurement team was limited. Only tacit approval was obtained for the procurement exemption. There were delays in issuing the final written contract. A subsequent modification to the contract did not have sufficient oversight by senior managers, as set out in the Council's Procurement Code.

findings.paper_title: Q4 Treasury Management Prudential Indicator report 2526

findings.paper_title: Outturn Cover report for PSC
findings.headline: Agency staff costs spent at 12 times budget (£602k vs £50k) indicating staffing constraints, with 27 vacancies unfilled due to 'recruitment challenges'.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £50k for agency staffing but spent £602k, a £552k overspend. This occurred despite 27 vacancies across departments, with the document noting overspends are 'due to recruitment challenges or service changes'. The vacancy savings of £1.2m masked this agency cost pressure.
findings.matters: Extreme agency cost overspend combined with unfilled vacancies suggests either recruitment problems or service delivery demands that cannot be met through permanent staffing, both indicators of organisational stress.
findings.figures: £602k agency spend vs £50k budget (£552k overspend), 27 unfilled vacancies, £1.2m salary underspend from vacancies
findings.quote: Overspends driven by increased spend on agency and casual staff across directorates have been partly mitigated by vacancy savings and unfilled posts, often due to recruitment challenges or service changes.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Outturn Cover report for PSC
findings.headline: Benefit claim processing times remain above the 11-day target at year-end despite improvement initiatives, a persistent red KPI.
findings.detail: Combined speed of processing for new benefit claims and change of circumstances has remained red throughout the year. Despite improvement initiatives, average processing time is not yet below the 11-day target. High volumes of correspondence continue to be received and are only partially mitigated by automation.
findings.matters: Persistent red KPI combined with the audit risk above suggests systemic resource constraints in this statutory function that have not been resolved.
findings.figures: Target 11 days, red status throughout year, high correspondence volumes
findings.quote: The KPIs for combined speed of processing for new benefit claims and change of circumstances has remained red throughout the year. The average processing time has slowly improved over the year but is not yet below the target of 11 days.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Outturn Cover report for PSC
findings.headline: LA error rate in benefit administration has marginal headroom before audit subsidy loss threshold, with loss explicitly flagged as 'a probability'.
findings.detail: The Quality Assurance LA error rate increased to 0.35%, below the 0.48% lower threshold but described as having only 'marginal headroom'. The council explicitly states it is 'more likely than not that any extrapolated audit findings would cause the Council to exceed the lower threshold at year-end', making subsidy loss 'a probability' rather than a remote risk.
findings.matters: A subsidy loss would be a direct financial penalty. This is not a contingent risk but an explicitly flagged probability that could materialize at next audit.
findings.figures: LA error rate 0.35%, lower threshold 0.48%, pre-audit figure with marginal headroom
findings.quote: The Quality Assurance: LA error rate has increased from 0.23% in quarter 3 to 0.35%, which is below the lower threshold. However, this remains a pre-audit figure with marginal headroom from the 0.48% lower threshold, and it is more likely than not that any extrapolated audit findings would cause the Council to exceed the lower threshold at year-end. Therefore, a loss of subsidy remains a probability, so the indicator remains red.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Outturn Cover report for PSC
findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits service overspent by £0.75m due to structural cost pressures including DWP migration and government subsidy caps.
findings.detail: The service exceeded budget by £0.75m driven by reduced recovery of benefit overpayments as working age cases migrate to the DWP, the government cap on subsidy for Supported Exempt Accommodation, reliance on temporary staffing, and increased customer correspondence volumes that automation only partially mitigates. These are systemic pressures rather than one-off costs.
findings.matters: This overspend is driven by external factors (DWP changes, government policy) that the council cannot control, suggesting structural underfunding of a statutory service.
findings.figures: £0.75m overspend, increased temporary staffing costs, high correspondence volumes
findings.quote: Revenues and Benefits service which exceeded budget by £0.75m. This reflects reduced recovery of benefit overpayments as working age cases migrate to the DWP for processing, the Government cap on subsidy for Supported Exempt Accommodation, as well as a reliance on temporary staffing earlier in the year increasing the contract costs.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: S106 and CIL developer contributions significantly underperformed expectations.
findings.detail: Only £180k of the £500k S106/CIL Infrastructure Spend budget was utilised, with the council explicitly citing lower than expected uptake. CIL processes are being reviewed.
findings.matters: Lower developer contribution income than budgeted may affect future infrastructure and affordable housing programmes, or force the council to self-fund schemes.
findings.figures: £180.2k actual vs £500k budget (36%)
findings.quote: Dependent on s106 bids. Spend reflects lower uptake. CIL processes underway reviewing future programme spend.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Vehicle procurement delayed by long lead times; £570k reprofiled to 2026/27.
findings.detail: Despite £1.95m approved budget, only £981k was spent (50%). The council explicitly notes long lead times have delayed delivery of vehicles on order, forcing £570k into the next year.
findings.matters: Procurement delays on fleet vehicles may impact waste collection and operational services; extended lead times reduce budget flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.94m budget; £981k spent (50%); £570k reprofiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: Vehicles on order but long lead times have caused delays with delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Blackhorse Way Improvement Scheme postponed to 2027/28 due to capacity constraints.
findings.detail: A £250k project was moved back a year during 2026/27 budget setting following a capacity review, suggesting the council identified resource constraints that forced reprioritisation.
findings.matters: Explicit capacity constraints mean the council may struggle to deliver planned programmes and could face further delays in strategic projects.
findings.figures: £250k budgeted; £0 spent; moved to 2027/28
findings.quote: Moved to 2027/28 following capacity review at 2026/27 budget setting.

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Housing acquisition programmes are progressing slower than budgeted.
findings.detail: Family Homes acquired only 3 of 10 properties (97% spent but 30% of properties purchased). Housing Enabling Grants spent only 56% of the £1.22m budget with works pushed to 2026/27. This suggests delivery constraints or funding delays from third parties.
findings.matters: Housing schemes are often critical to community wellbeing and council revenue targets; delays may signal capacity issues or third-party funding problems.
findings.figures: Family Homes: 3 of 10 properties purchased; Housing Enabling Grants: £686.6k vs £1.22m budget (56%)
findings.quote: Three of ten properties purchased. Remainder to be purchased in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Supply chain inflation is driving cost overruns on property works.
findings.detail: Housing Net Carbon Zero works overspent by 7% (£107k actual vs £100k budget), explicitly due to supply chain inflation. Park Street Flats Gas Boiler Removal also significantly overran at 145% of budget (£94.5k vs £65k).
findings.matters: Persistent inflationary pressure on construction and property works reduces budget predictability and may force reprioritisation or borrowing.
findings.figures: Housing Net Carbon Zero: £107.2k vs £100k budget; Park Street Flats: £94.5k vs £65k budget
findings.quote: Costs escalated due to supply chain inflation

findings.committee: Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix C Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Capitol Refurbishment significantly overran budget by £630k and is now constraining 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £2.276m for the Capitol Refurbishment, but spent £2.906m (128%). They attempted to reprofile £750k from the following year but it was insufficient. The overspend will now reduce 2026/27's budget allocation.
findings.matters: Material capital cost overruns that require future-year budget reductions signal either weak project governance or unforeseen project complexity that could recur.
findings.figures: £2.906m actual vs £2.276m budget (£630k overspend); Request to reprofile £750k was not enough
findings.quote: Construction works started and spend accelerated. Request to reprofile £750k from 2026/27 was not enough to cover 2025/26 spend. 2026/27 will be reduced by overspend here.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - Budget Funding Changes
findings.headline: General reserves depleted by £0.4m due to funding loss affecting capital programme
findings.detail: A previously anticipated £0.4m surplus that was planned to fund the capital programme can no longer be set aside. This £0.4m must now be drawn from general reserves instead, reducing the estimated reserve level from £10m to £9.6m by 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer for unexpected costs or emergencies; drawing them down to cover a one-time allocation shock reduces financial resilience.
findings.figures: £0.4m reduction; reserves drop from £10m to £9.6m by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: This £0.4m funding of the capital programme will now need to be funded from general reserves, reducing the estimated £10m reserve level at 31 March 2028 to £9.6m.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - Budget Funding Changes
findings.headline: Forced £0.5m savings plan required during 2026 to balance 2027/28 budget
findings.detail: The Council must develop and implement plans during 2026 to close a £0.5m deficit created by the funding reduction. This indicates the Council has no unallocated flexibility to absorb the funding loss and must find specific savings.
findings.matters: Shows the Council faces forced budget reductions with a defined gap to close, requiring difficult decisions about service cuts or efficiency savings.
findings.figures: £0.5m deficit to be closed in 2027/28
findings.quote: Plans should be undertaken during 2026 to reduce the anticipated £0.5m deficit as a result of this funding reduction so that the Council sets a balanced budget in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - Budget Funding Changes
findings.headline: £0.9m permanent funding reduction from 2027/28 and 2028/29 with no government compensation
findings.detail: A late government change to how business rates pooling gains are included in funding means the Council loses £0.9m in Core Spending Power. While a one-off £0.9m adjustment grant protects 2026/27, the Council receives no compensation for this change in 2027/28 and 2028/29, creating a permanent structural funding gap.
findings.matters: A material permanent reduction in funding forces difficult decisions about service levels or taxation, and reduces financial flexibility in future years.
findings.figures: £0.9m reduction in both 2027/28 and 2028/29; £0.9m one-off adjustment grant for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The one-off adjustment support grant is just for 2026/27, so there is no reimbursement for the Council for this change in 2027/28 or 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Housing company subsidiary loans create up to £9m contingent liability
findings.detail: The council plans to provide service loans up to £4m to its housing company subsidiary with additional loan commitments of £5m anticipated. While the council controls the subsidiary, service loans carry risk that the borrower cannot repay principal or interest. Housing company financial performance is therefore a material contingent liability.
findings.matters: Subsidiary lending increases total exposure and creates dependency on housing company performance, potentially requiring council support if the subsidiary encounters financial difficulties.
findings.figures: Service loan limit to housing company: £4m exposure; planned loan commitments: £5m; equity investment: £0.5m; total subsidiary exposure approaching £9.5m
findings.quote: The Council plans to provide loan commitments up to £4m to its Housing Company subsidiary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Investment portfolio funded by usable reserves and advance income, creating cash impact if values decline
findings.detail: The council has no borrowing and funds its £102.6m investment exposure from usable reserves and income received in advance of expenditure. This means if property values fall or income declines, the council must drawdown cash reserves to cover any shortfall or finance other operations.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded investment portfolio means any decline in values or income directly impacts cash available for operations, constraining the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Total investment exposure forecast 2026/27: £102.6m; funded entirely from reserves and advance income, no borrowing
findings.quote: Since the Council does not have any borrowing the Council's investments are funded by usable reserves and income received in advance of expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Portfolio security is narrow and conditional on values not falling below purchase cost
findings.detail: While the current portfolio valuation (£56.3m) exceeds historical purchase cost (£54.8m), providing £1.5m buffer, the council acknowledges valuation uncertainty. If 2025/26 audited values fall below purchase price, the Head of Property must review whether holding strategy is appropriate and report to Council with alternative actions.
findings.matters: The safety margin is slim (2.7% of portfolio) and if it erodes, the council's security position changes and it must consider alternative strategies for the £56m portfolio.
findings.figures: Current portfolio: £56.3m valuation vs £54.8m purchase cost = £1.5m margin (2.7%)
findings.quote: Should the audited values at the end of 2025/26 fall below their purchase price the Head of Property and Facilities will consider whether the current course of action of holding the assets is appropriate and bring any alternative actions to Council in an update to the Investment Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Swan Walk Centre demonstrates £8.4m unrealised loss in portfolio
findings.detail: The Swan Walk Centre equity investment was purchased for £9.5m and is currently valued at £1.1m, representing an £8.4m loss. This complex multiparty arrangement is highlighted separately because of its significant effect on the portfolio. The loss demonstrates material deterioration can occur and remain within a portfolio.
findings.matters: Swan Walk shows that commercial property investments can deteriorate significantly in value. It represents a locked-in loss and indicates inherent risks in complex property structures.
findings.figures: Swan Walk: £9.5m purchase cost, £1.1m current valuation, £8.4m loss (7.4% of total £126.6m investment exposure)
findings.quote: The major loss in value is due to the movement of the valuation of the Council's equity share in Swan Walk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio is under pressure from high interest rates and declining retail market
findings.detail: The council explicitly states property values have been pressured by high interest rates and economic uncertainty, with retail property values 'especially hard hit'. The £56.3m commercial property portfolio (valued above £54.8m purchase cost) is contingent on these market conditions continuing to support current valuations. Any deterioration in interest rates or retail market conditions poses direct risk.
findings.matters: Retail property is materially underperforming and if general property values decline further, the council's portfolio security erodes and income generation capacity diminishes, directly affecting budget balance.
findings.figures: Total commercial property £56.3m (£56m forecast 2026/27); retail holdings £12.7m (legacy £4.5m + recent £8.2m); net portfolio gain £1.5m
findings.quote: Property values have been under pressure from relatively high interest rates and doubts over the UK economy. Retail property values have been especially hard hit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(iii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Council is dependent on volatile commercial property income to achieve balanced budget
findings.detail: Horsham requires £3.7m of commercial property investment income (5% of the £73m gross service expenditure budget) to balance its 2026/27 budget. This dependency continues through the MTFS period (2027/28-2029/30) with planned income of £3.8-3.9m annually. The income is directly vulnerable to interest rate movements and commercial property market conditions.
findings.matters: If commercial property values fall or income declines, the council faces a structural gap in its revenue budget, forcing reserve drawdowns or service cuts.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £3.7m investment income out of £73m gross service expenditure (5%); forecast 2027/28 £3.8m, 2028/29 £3.9m
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: CFO advises existing resources must be reshaped rather than expanded, signalling structural not cyclical budget pressure
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states the Council must not spend more than affordable without compensating savings, and should 'reshape' existing resources rather than add capacity. This language indicates the CFO views the challenge as structural—requiring service restructuring and difficult choices—not manageable through incremental efficiency.
findings.matters: A CFO signalling the need to reshape services rather than find incremental savings suggests material structural change ahead, including possible service reductions or reorganisation, which impacts service continuity and risk.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Additional spending now without financial return or extra income and / or savings to compensate will only sharpen the need for deeper cuts or much higher fees and charges increases later. The Chief Finance Officer therefore advises that existing resources are reshaped, rather than added to.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: CFO warns forced borrowing will add material revenue strain through debt service and Minimum Revenue Provision charges
findings.detail: Once reserves are spent down to minimum, the Council will shift from internally-funded capital to external borrowing. The CFO explicitly warns this 'would greatly add to the revenue strain through borrowing costs and the Minimum Revenue Provision,' creating a negative feedback loop where debt service worsens the structural deficit.
findings.matters: Forced borrowing due to reserve exhaustion increases permanent revenue costs, eroding debt service coverage and signalling deteriorating creditworthiness to lenders.
findings.figures: Borrowing costs and MRP charges unquantified but flagged as material
findings.quote: at which point the Council would have to borrow the money, rather than internally source. This would greatly add to the revenue strain through borrowing costs and the Minimum Revenue Provision.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Plan depends on unspecified transformation funding, income generation, and efficiencies not embedded in service plans
findings.detail: Financial forecasts assume £0.2m annual transformation funding, unspecified income growth, fee increases, and efficiency savings. Critically, the CFO notes 'this action is no longer set out in the 2026/27 annual plan', meaning these savings are not formally allocated to service areas or validated.
findings.matters: Unspecified and unembedded savings represent downside risk; if transformation targets slip or income initiatives underperform, reserve depletion accelerates and structural deficit arrives earlier than forecast.
findings.figures: £0.2m transformation funding annually; income and efficiency targets unquantified and unplanned
findings.quote: It also assumes the Council uses £0.2m of transformation funding each year alongside a combination of generating more income, raising fees and seeking the usual efficiencies in existing expenditure and resources. Should that not be the case, then the level of general fund reserves would further decline. This action is no longer set out in the 2026/27 annual plan however.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Leisure and wellbeing contract investment costs unquantified in current forecasts; £3m reserve set aside but full exposure unknown
findings.detail: The Council is investing in a new leisure and wellbeing contract but the CFO explicitly states 'the current assumptions do not include the impact of further significant investment in the leisure centres as part of the leisure and wellbeing contract reletting.' A £3m initial reserve is allocated, but full investment costs are unpriced and could accelerate reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Unquantified capital commitments create hidden downside risk; if leisure centre investment exceeds £3m, reserves deplete faster and the timeline to structural deficit shortens materially.
findings.figures: £3m initial leisure reserve; full investment cost unspecified
findings.quote: The current assumptions do not include the impact of further significant investment in the leisure centres as part of the leisure and wellbeing contract reletting. The level of reserves would decrease at an even faster rate as further capital expenditure is spent down to the minimum level of reserves

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Capital programme consuming £16.4m from General Fund reserves over three years, front-loading reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The Council is funding capital expenditure directly from reserves rather than borrowing or external funding: £3.5m in 2025/26, £7.9m in 2026/27, and £5m in 2027/28. This front-loaded depletion leaves minimal headroom for additional investment, volatility, or contingencies.
findings.matters: Funding capital from reserves rather than borrowing reduces financial flexibility and accelerates the path to minimum reserves, constraining future investment capacity and signalling debt aversion rather than prudent capital management.
findings.figures: £16.4m total capital funding from reserves: £3.5m (2025/26), £7.9m (2026/27), £5m (2027/28)
findings.quote: the impact of funding the large capital programme will consume around £16.4m of the General Fund balance across 2025/26 (£3.5m), 2026/27 (£7.9m) and 2027/28 (£5m)

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: £5m structural deficit cliff-edge forecast for 2029/30 with no identified bridging plan
findings.detail: The paper explicitly forecasts a £5m cliff-edge deficit in 2029/30—a multi-year structural imbalance between recurring income and expenditure, not a cyclical pressure. With reserves already depleted to near-minimum levels, this deficit has no financial cushion and no documented resolution pathway.
findings.matters: A £5m structural deficit represents unsustainable finances; resolving it requires material service reductions, tax increases, or emergency borrowing, any of which signals credit deterioration.
findings.figures: £5m cliff-edge deficit in 2029/30
findings.quote: this would leave a general fund balance of £10m by 31 March 2028, which is over the £6m minimum level but with little headroom to be able to add any investment into the leisure and wellbeing contract from general reserves, nor protect the new unitary authority from the £5m cliff-edge forecast deficit in 2029/30

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: General reserves falling from £24.8m to £4.1m by 2030, breaching the £6m minimum safety threshold by 2029/30
findings.detail: Reserves decline from £24.8m (March 2025) to £10m (March 2028), then continue falling to £4.1m by 2030. The Council targets a £6m minimum level for resilience; falling below this leaves the Council exposed to unplanned costs or income volatility. The trajectory shows relentless deterioration with little time to course-correct.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion below safety thresholds signals inability to absorb shocks and forces the Council toward borrowing, materially worsening debt service coverage and financial resilience.
findings.figures: General reserves: £24.8m (March 2025), £10m (March 2028), £4.1m (2030); minimum threshold £6m
findings.quote: General reserves at 31 March 2025 were £24.8m. However, as the graph below indicates, the impact of funding the large capital programme will consume around £16.4m of the General Fund balance across 2025/26 (£3.5m), 2026/27 (£7.9m) and 2027/28 (£5m). After adding in the forecast revenue surpluses in 2026/27 and 2027/28, this would leave a general fund balance of £10m by 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(ii) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Useable reserves projected to fall from £97.4m to £55.2m (43% decline) by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's useable reserves are forecast to decline from £97.4m in 2024/25 to £55.2m by 2028/29, with investment balances falling from £70.0m to £31.5m over the same period. The document attributes this to reserves being used to finance capital expenditure and developer contributions flowing out. Even at the lowest point, the council expects to maintain £31.5m in investments.
findings.matters: A 43% reduction in reserves over four years affects the council's financial buffer and capacity to absorb unexpected revenue shortfalls or capital pressures
findings.figures: Useable reserves falling from £97.4m (2024/25 actual) to £55.2m (2028/29 estimate); investments falling from £70.0m to £31.5m
findings.quote: Investments levels are expected to fall over the period as reserves are used to finance capital spend and developer contributions flow out.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(i) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: 22% of net revenue budget depends on £56m commercial property portfolio yielding 7.3%, with acknowledged property market risks
findings.detail: The council holds £56m in commercial property investments generating 7.3% net return, providing £3.7m income in 2026/27 (representing 22% of net revenue stream). The council acknowledges higher risks on commercial investment—individual vacancies, falls in market value, economic factors—and holds only £6m general reserves as a buffer for income shortfalls.
findings.matters: Over one-fifth of the council's revenue budget depends on volatile commercial property income. While a £6m buffer is held, a material portion of core revenue is exposed to property market cycles and individual asset performance. A downturn could force service reductions or accelerate reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Commercial property holdings £56m (valued 31.3.2025); net return 7.3%; net income £3.7m (2026/27 budget); proportion of net revenue stream 22% (2026/27), declining to 19% by 2028/29; £6m general reserves buffer for income shortfalls
findings.quote: To support its services the Council invests in commercial property. Commercial property investments were valued at £56m on 31 March 2025 and they provided a net return after direct costs of 7.3%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E(i) for 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Cash reserves depleting 54% over MTFS period (£70m to £32m) as capital programme is financed from internal resources
findings.detail: The council is increasing capital expenditure to £21.0m in 2026/27 (up 43% from £14.7m forecast for 2025/26) and financing this from reserves rather than external borrowing. Total cash balances decline from £70m at March 2025 to £46m by March 2027 and £32m by March 2029. The council states this will reduce longer-term cash balances.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion erodes the council's financial buffer and reduces capacity for internal borrowing to manage unexpected pressures or capital emergencies. Lenders would be concerned about the trajectory of balance sheet cash and implications for financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Cash reserves: £70m (31.3.2025 actual) falling to £46m (31.3.2027) and £32m (31.3.2029); capital spend increasing from £14.7m (2025/26 forecast) to £21.0m (2026/27); internal resource financing £9.9m (2025/26) to £12.0m (2026/27)
findings.quote: The increased spend will be financed from reserves which will reduce longer term cash balances.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in 2028 creates strategic uncertainty affecting all medium-term financial planning
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: "We do not yet know how the impact and timescale of Local Government Reorganisation may affect funding over the period of a multi-year settlement, especially if Horsham District Council ceases to exist in 2028. We also don't know how it will affect the ability to pool Business Rates in West Sussex beyond 31 March 2028." The paper notes that LGR creates uncertainty for the leisure contract relet (December 2027, before any possible reorganisation), additional workload on officers, and the risk of staff departures due to uncertainty. The MTFS projects deficits to 2029/30, but "the medium-term might be deemed irrelevant for the present Council" if LGR occurs as planned.
findings.matters: LGR creates fundamental uncertainty about whether the council will exist beyond 2028, whether its financial commitments will transfer to a new authority, and whether the financial position modelled in the MTFS will ever be realised. This is material uncertainty for a lender assessing the authority's ability to deliver medium-term plans.
findings.figures: Possible reorganisation date: 2028; current MTFS extends to 2029/30; three-year settlement covers period until 2028/29; large capital and revenue commitments extend through 2027/28
findings.quote: We do not yet know how the impact and timescale of Local Government Reorganisation may affect funding over the period of a multi-year settlement, especially if Horsham District Council ceases to exist in 2028

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Government funding reduction of 4.3% (£1m) in Core Spending Power, described as "most redistributive in recent times", placing council in top quartile of cuts
findings.detail: The council is one of 50-60 authorities facing cuts of up to 5% in Core Spending Power. MHCLG justified these cuts on the basis that affected councils have benefited from business rate growth, have high levels of reserves, and had advance warning of cuts signalled years ago. Horsham's Core Spending Power fell from £24.765m (2025/26) to £23.694m (2026/27), a reduction of £1.07m or 4.3%. Additionally, Government expects councils to raise the maximum council tax (2.99%), which the council notes places "a further £0.5m strain on residents locally each year, totalling a further £1.5m reduction in Government grants overall." This equates to a 10.1% reduction in total Government funding over three years.
findings.matters: This signals a fundamental shift in Government funding philosophy away from grant funding toward local taxation and self-reliance. Councils in lower-income areas with weaker tax bases face structural pressures as funding continues to shift.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power 2026/27: £23.694m, down £1.07m (4.3%) from 2025/26; further £1.5m reduction if Government expects 2.99% council tax increases over three years; total 10.1% reduction in Government funding
findings.quote: Government has reduced the Council's Core Spending Power by £1m (4.3%) compared to 2025/26. This Council are one of 50 to 60 authorities facing cuts of up to 5%

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: West Sussex Business Rates pool disbanded for 2026/27 after baseline reset created unquantified risk of loss
findings.detail: The council participated in a West Sussex Business Rates pool in 2025/26 and benefited from growth income above the baseline. However, Government reset the Business Rates baseline for 2026/27, meaning all previous growth is lost. The re-baselining also removes the pool's surplus buffer, creating genuine risk of the pool incurring a cost to Government rather than generating growth. West Sussex Chief Finance Officers collectively concluded "that based on the current, imperfect data, a Pool in 2026/27 would be unviable, as it would more likely than not end up in a loss overall and a payment to Government." The council therefore left the pool, losing access to potential growth income.
findings.matters: This represents a loss of a previously available income stream due to Government rebaselining policy. The council can no longer access pooling benefits, and re-baselining will happen more regularly going forward, meaning "future growth will be banked by Government rather than locally."
findings.figures: Business Rates retained: £2.8m (6% of £45m collected); Baseline reset 2026/27; pool decision deadline 14 January 2026; re-baselining to recur regularly
findings.quote: Government has reset the business rates baseline for 2026/27 meaning that all previous growth is lost. The re-baselining also means there is a greater risk of a cost to the Pool as there is no built-up surplus buffer to insulate against the loss

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Potential £15m leisure facility investment required for 2027/28 contract relet, adding £0.6m annual revenue cost not yet in MTFS
findings.detail: The council's four leisure facilities (Broadbridge Heath, Billingshurst, Horsham Pavilions, Steyning) will be subject to a contract relet in December 2027. Three of the four are several years old and likely to need investment. A consultant is currently developing a business case for facility investment. The council estimates that spending £15m on leisure investment "could be as much as £0.6m p.a. based on a 4% cost of capital." Importantly, these costs are "not yet been included in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy modelling but will need to be factored into any future decision making." This represents a material unquantified future liability.
findings.matters: The council has not yet finalized a significant capital commitment (£15m) that would materially worsen the revenue position (additional £0.6m p.a. cost pressure) in a period when the MTFS already shows structural deficits. This creates uncertainty around actual future financial position.
findings.figures: Indicative £15m leisure investment; potential revenue impact £0.6m p.a.; contract relet December 2027; Cabinet to report on business case March 2026
findings.quote: The revenue impact from spending an indicative £15m on the investment could be as much as £0.6m p.a. based on a 4% cost of capital. In addition, it is likely that some of the facilities would close for periods during a refurbishment

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Supported accommodation subsidy pressures (£0.47m additional cost in 2026/27) are growing and likely to persist
findings.detail: The council faces higher costs in Housing Benefit from subsidised accommodation properties capped for subsidy under Government policy, combined with lower recovery of overpayments as customers shift from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit. These pressures are identified in the budget and are not a one-off; they reflect structural changes in welfare administration that will continue. The paper notes these as part of ongoing service demand pressures in 2026/27.
findings.matters: These costs are driven by policy changes beyond the council's control (Universal Credit migration) and by claimants with more complex needs in higher-cost accommodation. They represent a structural increase in the council's housing support burden.
findings.figures: £0.47m additional cost in Revenues and Benefits for supported and exempt accommodation in 2026/27
findings.quote: higher costs of £0.47m are being felt in Revenues and Benefits from higher Supported and Exempt Accommodation costs which are properties that often involve claimants with more complex needs in the light of rising mental health and addiction problems, that are capped for subsidy

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant income (£2m in 2026/27) is forecast to decline 10% annually as producers adapt
findings.detail: The council received £2.3m in EPR funding for 2025/26 and is budgeting £2m for 2026/27. The MTFS assumes a 10% annual reduction based on the decline from 2025/26 to 2026/27, anticipating that producers will reduce packaging to avoid the tax. The council states: "It is likely that Extended Producer Responsibility for Packaging funding will fall in the future with the theory that producers will look to reduce packaging to avoid these costs." This creates a falling revenue stream that is already built into projected deficits.
findings.matters: Declining income without corresponding expenditure reductions worsens the structural budget position. This is a volatile, uncertain income source the council is relying on to help balance the MTFS.
findings.figures: £2.0m EPR grant 2026/27 declining 10% annually; £2.3m received in 2025/26; total decline from 2025/26 to 2026/27: £0.3m (13%)
findings.quote: The Council received £2.3m in 2025/26, so the Medium-Term financial Strategy is currently assuming a 10% reduction each year

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Food waste collection (£2m annual ongoing cost) is funded through declining Revenue Support Grant, creating structural budget pressure
findings.detail: The Government bundled food waste funding into the Revenue Support Grant without specifying the amount, and the RSG is forecast to fall from £7.479m in 2026/27 to £5.358m in 2027/28 to £3.174m in 2028/29. The paper notes: "Wrapping the funding into the Revenue Support Grant is detrimental because the three-year settlement shows the level of RSG reducing significantly over the next two financial years." Food waste costs will only rise from inflation and salaries, meaning the council absorbs an increasing share of the cost. This is "a significant contributory factor towards the financial deficit in the later years of the Medium-Term Financial Strategy, once the transitional protection funding ends."
findings.matters: This is an unfunded mandate imposed by Government that will structurally worsen the council's position. As RSG declines, the food waste burden automatically shifts more of its cost onto the council, creating a predictable future shortfall.
findings.figures: £2m annual ongoing cost for food waste collection; RSG declining from £7.479m (2026/27) to £3.174m (2028/29); transitional protection ends after 2028/29
findings.quote: Wrapping the funding into the Revenue Support Grant is detrimental because the three-year settlement shows the level of RSG reducing significantly over the next two financial years

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: General fund reserves will fall from £24.8m to £10m by March 2028, leaving minimal headroom above the £6m minimum
findings.detail: The council's large capital programme (£26.7m in 2026/27, £8.3m in 2027/28) will consume £16.4m of the general fund balance (£3.5m in 2025/26, £7.9m in 2026/27, £5m in 2027/28). Even after accounting for revenue surpluses, the general fund will be at £10m by March 2028 with "little headroom to be able to add any investment into the leisure and wellbeing contract from general reserves." The Chief Finance Officer cautions that "it is advisable not to spend extra money now without return today that may be needed in the future."
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces financial flexibility and the council's ability to respond to unexpected pressures or shocks. A lender assesses reserve adequacy as a key buffer against financial distress.
findings.figures: General fund balance: £24.8m (31 March 2025) declining to £10m (31 March 2028); minimum reserve level: £6m; capital programme 2026/27-2027/28: £35m total
findings.quote: After adding in the forecast revenue surpluses in 2026/27 and 2027/28, this would leave a general fund balance of £10m by 31 March 2028, which is over the £6m minimum level but with little headroom

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Budget deficit emerges in 2028/29 despite current surplus, driven by cost pressures outpacing funding growth
findings.detail: The council achieves a £1.6m surplus in 2026/27 after capital funding and a £0.4m surplus in 2027/28, but the MTFS projects a deficit of £0.12m in 2028/29 and £5.4m in 2029/30. This deterioration reflects Government funding growing at only 0.1% per year while service costs continue to grow. The council notes that "the combination of a growing net cost of service, reduction in funding and a high level of capital spending will strain revenue and reserves in the future."
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of the council's finances and whether deficits ahead are sustainable or signal structural problems that cannot be bridged.
findings.figures: Budget deficit of £0.12m in 2028/29, escalating to £5.415m in 2029/30; Core Spending Power reduced by £1.0m (4.3%) in 2026/27; funding growth of only 0.1% combined with expenditure pressures
findings.quote: a funding growth of only 0.1% combined with expenditure pressures creates a net deficit in later years estimated at £0.12m in 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy Appendix C IInvestment Strategy
findings.headline: Council has contingency trigger to review investment strategy if property valuations fall below purchase cost by end of 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's security test defines investment properties as secure only if their accounting valuation remains at or above purchase cost. The portfolio currently meets this test but the strategy commits that if audited values at year-end 2025/26 fall below purchase price, the Head of Property and Facilities will consider alternative courses of action and bring updates to Council. This trigger is material because retail valuations are already under pressure and the council may be forced into asset sales or strategy revision if declines continue.
findings.matters: The trigger indicates the council recognises risk of further property value deterioration and is prepared to take action (potentially including asset sales) if the current surplus is eroded, signalling stress management but also implying limited financial headroom in the portfolio
findings.figures: Current portfolio surplus above purchase cost: £1.5m (£56.3m value vs £54.8m cost). Revaluation occurs annually by external valuer. Trigger point: any value below £54.8m purchase cost.
findings.quote: should the audited values at the end of 2025/26 fall below their purchase price the Head of Property and Facilities will consider whether the current course of action of holding the assets is appropriate and bring any alternative actions to Council

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy Appendix C IInvestment Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio, especially retail investments, shows cumulative losses from valuation declines and Swan Walk Centre has £8.4m unrealised loss
findings.detail: The council holds £56.3m in commercial property with £13.8m invested in retail. Retail properties carry cumulative unrealised losses of £13.1m from their original cost (Swan Walk alone: £8.4m loss on £9.5m purchase; recent retail purchases: £6.5m loss on £14.7m). The strategy acknowledges property values have been under pressure from high interest rates and economic uncertainty, with retail especially hard hit. Portfolio is currently valued above purchase cost by £1.5m but this assumes values broadly hold their value amid acknowledged uncertainty.
findings.matters: Unrealised losses reduce buffer above purchase cost and if combined with further market pressure could require asset sales or trigger valuation below purchase cost, forcing the council to consider alternative strategies
findings.figures: Swan Walk: £9.5m purchase cost, £1.1m current value (£8.4m loss). Retail recent: £14.7m purchase cost, £8.2m value (£6.5m loss). Total portfolio: £54.8m purchase cost, £56.3m current value (£1.5m surplus). Retail represents £13.8m of total portfolio.
findings.quote: Property values have been under pressure from relatively high interest rates and doubts over the UK economy. Retail property values have been especially hard hit.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy Appendix C IInvestment Strategy
findings.headline: Council's revenue budget is dependent on declining investment income while service expenditure grows, creating structural vulnerability
findings.detail: The council's gross service expenditure is forecast to rise from £68m (2024/25) to £73m (2026/27), whilst investment income is falling from £4.1m to £3.7m. Investment income provides 5–6% of the gross service budget across the medium-term forecast period. The strategy explicitly recognises this dependency and the figures represent best estimates bearing in mind challenging economic conditions, implying the council has limited flexibility if investment returns deteriorate further.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can sustain its revenue budget if investment returns fall further, as this represents a structural vulnerability in budget formation that cannot be easily addressed through service reductions
findings.figures: Gross service expenditure 2024/25: £68m, 2026/27: £73m. Investment income 2024/25: £4.1m (6% of budget), 2026/27: £3.7m (5% of budget). Forecasts 2027/28-2028/29 maintain 5% dependency.
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy Appendix B Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Useable reserves projected to decline 43% from £97.4m to £55.2m over four years as capital spending is financed from cash balances
findings.detail: The Council forecasts useable reserves falling from £97.4m (actual 2024/25) to £55.2m (estimate 2028/29), with estimated investments declining from £70m to £31.5m. This reflects the strategy of financing capital expenditure from internal cash resources rather than external borrowing. Current general revenue reserves of £25m as at 31 March 2025 remain above the minimum target of £6m, providing a £19m buffer, but the trajectory shows material balance sheet depletion over the period.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion rates signal the runway available for capital programmes and the flexibility remaining for unexpected events; lenders assess reserve adequacy and drawdown trajectory as indicators of financial resilience.
findings.figures: Useable reserves decline from £97.4m to £55.2m; estimated investments from £70m to £31.5m; general revenue reserves £25m against £6m minimum target
findings.quote: Investments levels are expected to fall over the period as reserves are used to finance capital spend and developer contributions flow out.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Internal borrowing strategy is sustainable only in the medium term; Director flagging potential need for external borrowing.
findings.detail: The council relies on internal borrowing—using reserves and cash resources rather than external debt—to finance the capital programme. The Director of Resources states this approach is 'sustainable in the medium term' but commits to monitoring it 'in order to be ready to respond should external borrowing become advisable.'
findings.matters: The qualifier 'medium term' signals financial stress beyond the current plan horizon. If external borrowing becomes necessary, rates of 4.5%–5.8% would add material financing costs to an already-strained revenue budget and further constrain the successor authority.
findings.figures: Projected external debt declining from £5.9m (2025/26) to £5.1m (2028/29); potential borrowing rates 4.5% short-term, 5.8% long-term
findings.quote: From projections of the capital programme and use of reserves this strategy is seen as sustainable in the medium term although the Director of Resources will monitor the actual position against the projections in order to be ready to respond should external borrowing become advisable.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio income—currently 29% of net revenue stream—faces persistent risks, particularly in retail sector.
findings.detail: The council holds a commercial property portfolio valued at £56m, generating £4.1m net income in 2024/25 (7.3% yield). The strategy projects income will be maintained but explicitly identifies 'persistent' risks, particularly in retail. Principal exposures include individual voids, falls in market value, and changes in economic activity. The council relies on at least £6m of general reserves to absorb shortfalls.
findings.matters: Commercial property income represents a material share of net revenue. Income volatility here, especially in a weakened retail environment, could impact the council's ability to meet revenue commitments as reserves are depleted.
findings.figures: Commercial portfolio £56m; 7.3% net yield 2024/25; £4.1m net income; 29% of net revenue stream
findings.quote: The commercial property portfolio is projected to maintain income levels but risks to income persist especially in the retail part of the portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Investment income will fall by £400,000 as a direct result of reserve depletion funding the capital programme.
findings.detail: As reserves are drawn down to fund capital expenditure, cash balances available for investment will be greatly reduced. This results in lower investment income: from £3.4m budgeted for 2025/26 down to £3.0m for 2026/27. This income compression occurs precisely when the council is most stressed financially.
findings.matters: Reduced investment income further constrains financial flexibility at a time when the council is depleting its reserves and preparing for organizational transition.
findings.figures: 2025/26 investment income £3.4m; 2026/27 budget £3.0m; shortfall £0.4m
findings.quote: Investment income will be reduced as cash levels will have been greatly reduced.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026 27 incorp Investment Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Capital programme of £30m will significantly deplete reserves, leaving the council in a much weakened financial position.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme stands at over £30m, described as 'much higher than the usual level'. To finance this, a significant portion of the council's reserves will be used. While reserves are projected to remain above the £6m minimum level, the council explicitly acknowledges this will leave it in a 'much weakened financial position' as it hands over to its successor body.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce financial resilience and the council's capacity to manage unexpected pressures or support its successor authority during transition.
findings.figures: £30m capital programme; £6m minimum reserve level; reserves will be 'greatly reduced'
findings.quote: To finance this a significant portion of the Council's reserves will have to be used leaving it in a much weakened financial position as it hands over to a successor body.

findings.paper_title: 25 HDC Audit results report - FINAL
findings.headline: Pension asset overstatement of £0.58m identified but not corrected by management
findings.detail: The West Sussex Pension Fund auditor identified a £0.58m overstatement in the council's pension assets due to changes in pension asset values. Management chose not to correct this, deciding it was immaterial on a judgemental basis.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements, even individually judged as immaterial, accumulate risk. Pension liabilities are typically material to council balance sheets, and declining to correct them signals weak governance discipline.
findings.figures: £0.58m uncorrected pension asset overstatement
findings.quote: The pensions fund auditor also identified a £0.58m overstatement of assets due changes in pension asset values. Management have not corrected for this judgemental misstatement on the basis of materiality.

findings.paper_title: 25 HDC Audit results report - FINAL
findings.headline: Housing asset valuations contain £0.85m error; £0.09m remains uncorrected in current year
findings.detail: Housing assets valued in 2023/24 used incorrect methodology (wrong application of vacant possession criteria). Total error identified was £0.85m. Management corrected £0.76m through 2024/25 revaluation but left £0.09m uncorrected, citing materiality grounds.
findings.matters: Systemic valuation methodology errors across multiple asset classes (housing and car parks) indicate the council's valuation control environment is weak. Uncorrected misstatements compound audit risk and signal governance issues.
findings.figures: £0.85m total error; £0.09m left uncorrected in 2024/25
findings.quote: the valuation methodology for housing assets valued in 2023/24 was incorrect as the valuer incorrectly applied the vacant possession criteria in 2023/24 when the valuation guidance had changed in October 2024. Management have calculated the 2023/24 misstatement amount to £0.85m and have not corrected for this misstatement due to materiality... resulting in £0.76m misstatement being corrected through the 2024/25 valuation with remaining £0.09m misstatement left uncorrected.

findings.paper_title: 25 HDC Audit results report - FINAL
findings.headline: Material error in car park valuations identified by EY specialists
findings.detail: EY Real Estate specialists identified that the valuation methodology for car parks (£24.7m asset value) was incorrect due to wrong income and yield assumptions applied in 2024/25. The council is recalculating the adjustment needed, including a prior period correction.
findings.matters: Material valuation errors in income-generating assets directly misstate the balance sheet and suggest weak control over engagement with valuers. Car parks generate revenue — methodology failures here indicate governance gaps in capital asset management.
findings.figures: £24.7m in car park valuations affected by material methodology error
findings.quote: the valuation methodology for car parks valued in 2024/25 with a value of £24.7m was incorrect due to the income and yield used, resulting in a material misstatement. The Council are currently calculating the car park valuation adjustment (including prior period adjustment).

findings.paper_title: 25 HDC Audit results report - FINAL
findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements
findings.detail: EY cannot express an opinion on whether the financial statements are true and fair. They lack sufficient audit evidence over £116.2m in property valuations revalued in 2022/23 and £75.5m in reserves classification, stemming from prior-year disclaimer opinions (2022/23 and 2023/24 both disclaimed). This is part of the national audit backlog recovery programme with a backstop date of 27 February 2026.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means no independent verification that the council's accounts present a true position of its financial state. This is a critical red flag for any lender assessing creditworthiness and represents unresolved audit gaps spanning three years.
findings.figures: £116,172,000 lacking audit evidence over valuations; £75,452,000 lacking evidence over reserves classification
findings.quote: we do not have sufficient appropriate audit evidence over: the valuation of property, plant and equipment that were revalued in the financial year 2022/23, amounting to £116,172,000, and the total of reserves and their classification except for the pensions reserve and the accumulated absences reserve, amounting to £75,452,000.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: 2025/26 budget forecast balanced only because of higher-than-budget parking, planning and treasury income; any shortfall will be funded from reserves
findings.detail: The £0.5m Revenues & Benefits overspend is being offset by better-than-forecast income from parking, planning, and treasury. If this income does not materialise, overspend goes to reserves. This is fragile: a downturn in discretionary spending or interest rates could flip to deficit.
findings.matters: Current year balance is dependent on income assumptions, not structural; reserve funding of any gap is already the plan, signalling low margin for error.
findings.figures: £0.5m Revenues & Benefits overspend offset by higher parking, planning and treasury management volumes
findings.quote: However higher parking, planning and treasury management volumes have increased income, such that the forecast for the overall funding position in 2025/26 is a balanced budget, able to absorb the unfunded £0.5m expenditure subsequently added to the budget. Should this not be the eventual outturn, any overspend will be funded from general fund reserve.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Weekly food waste collection mandate: £2m annual ongoing cost with only partial government funding certainty
findings.detail: Government-mandated weekly food waste collection from March 2026. £2.6m capital cost (only £1.5m government grant, so 57% covered). £2m annual revenue cost; government has not confirmed ongoing grant. Council set aside £4m in earmarked reserves to cover shortfall. Implementation risk: costs may overrun and reserve assumptions may not hold.
findings.matters: A large, unfunded service mandate creates structural revenue cost with uncertain government support; council is self-funding a government programme with reserves.
findings.figures: £2m annual revenue cost for food waste collection; £2.6m capital cost with £1.5m government grant; £4m earmarked reserve set aside (£1.3m + £0.3m + £2.4m from three years' settlements)
findings.quote: Government has not yet indicated what, if any, ongoing revenue grant will be distributed towards the anticipated ongoing £2m annual revenue cost for a weekly food waste collection service.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Investment income of £3.6m forecast for 2025/26 but declining: interest rates forecast to fall from 4% to 3.75% by 2026
findings.detail: Council relies on investment income to balance current budget. Interest rate cuts will reduce this income. Current forecast £3.6m (£0.2m above budget), but as rates decline and capital is deployed, this income will shrink. CFO warns this puts council 'at risk of a widening deficit if the interest rate falls'.
findings.matters: A key income source is declining due to macro conditions beyond council control; council is dependent on asset yields to balance operations, a fragile strategy.
findings.figures: £3.6m investment income forecast 2025/26; Bank of England base rate forecast to level out at 3.75% in 2026 (down from 4%)
findings.quote: Being reliant on investment income though puts the Council at risk of a widening deficit if the interest rate falls or if the investments are spent on something that generates a lower return than Treasury Management.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits service forecast to exceed budget by £0.5m in 2025/26 (forecast at month 6)
findings.detail: Service overspending: reduced ability to recover overpayments due to Universal Credit migration, high volume of supported accommodation (subsidy capped), increased temporary staff costs. This is a known structural pressure from government policy change, not a one-off.
findings.matters: An in-year service overspend signals pressure and loss of control; Universal Credit migration will continue to impact this service, making recovery difficult.
findings.figures: £0.5m overspend forecast at month 6 2025/26
findings.quote: The 2024/25 outturn indicated significant cost pressures in Revenues and Benefits which are also feeding through in 2025/26. At month 6, the service is forecast to exceed budget by £0.5m. This is due to a reduction in the ability to recover overpayments as working-age claimants are migrated to the DWP for processing under Universal Credit

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: General Fund reserves declining: £26.4m (March 2023) → £24.8m (March 2025), expected to drop further in 2026/27
findings.detail: Reserves have fallen £1.6m in two years and are forecast to continue declining as capital is spent. Minimum reserve policy is £6m, leaving £18.8m buffer. At current trajectory of £30m capital spend, reserves will erode quickly.
findings.matters: Shrinking reserves reduce financial flexibility and borrowing capacity if revenue position deteriorates; minimum reserves may become binding constraint.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £26.4m at 31 March 2023, £24.8m at 31 March 2025; minimum £6m
findings.quote: The level of reserves has remained fairly constant, with a General Fund balance of £26.4m at 31 March 2023 falling to £24.8m at 31 March 2025. The balance is expected to dip during 2025/26 and drop off in 2026/27 as the capital is spent.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: 63% of £30.1m 2026/27 capital programme funded from revenue and reserves (up from 51% in 2025/26)
findings.detail: Capital programme growing: £15.9m in 2025/26 (51% from revenue/reserves) to £30.1m in 2026/27 (63% from revenue/reserves, £18.8m). Most capital projects do not generate financial return. This revenue-funded capital is unsustainable and will accelerate reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Heavy borrowing-equivalent through reserves is not fiscally sustainable; council is trading endowment for current spending, weakening long-term position.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital programme £30.1m with £18.8m (63%) funded from revenue and reserves, compared to £15.9m in 2025/26 with £8.1m (51%) from revenue/reserves
findings.quote: It is important to recognise the impact that this has on the Council's revenue finances, as the majority of capital projects do not deliver a financial return on investment. The capital programme has been partly funded by reserves and other income not taken into revenue.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Government settlement funding cut of up to 7% (£0.7m minimum, potentially £4.6m total impact in 2026/27)
findings.detail: Council informed by MHCLG it is one of 49 authorities facing a 7% cut in Settlement Funding Assessment. The baseline cut is £0.7m, but if food waste grant (£2m) and Extended Producer Responsibility (£1.9m) are rolled into the consolidated grant before reductions, the total loss could be £2.6m to £4.6m in 2026/27 alone. The formulae have not been shared.
findings.matters: Material revenue loss with high uncertainty: the council cannot model the true impact until December 2025 Provisional Settlement, creating strategic planning risk.
findings.figures: 7% reduction in Settlement Funding Assessment compared to 2025/26, approximately £0.7m, though could be £2.6m to £4.6m worse off in 2026/27 depending on grant consolidation
findings.quote: we are one of 49 authorities likely to receive a 7% cut in Settlement Funding Assessment grants (compared to 2025/26). This could reduce our income by around £0.7m, although it could be more if other grants are rolled into the Settlement Funding Assessment pot before the reductions are made.

findings.paper_title: Update on the Council's financial position in 2025/26 and MTFS 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.headline: Predicted £1.4m annual budget deficit by 2028/29 with no savings plan yet commissioned
findings.detail: The medium-term financial strategy projects deficits of £1.4m by 2028/29, but the council is not currently working on savings plans because councillors are reluctant to plan ahead of Local Government Reorganisation. The Chief Finance Officer warns that reserves 'can only be spent once' and that further cuts or fee increases will be needed later if this materialises.
findings.matters: A council on trajectory to deficits without a prepared response is a credit risk; reliance on future cuts or fee rises to balance is procyclical and reduces borrowing headroom.
findings.figures: £1.4m deficit forecast for 2028/29; £1.4m deficit to find each year by end of 2027/28
findings.quote: current Medium-Term Financial Strategy projections produce a £1.4m deficit to find each year by the end of 2027/28. Plans for future savings are not currently being worked on as Councillors are reluctant to do this prior to Local Government Reorganisation.
